query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A minor alloying addition of aluminum (~2 at.%) to cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxygen resistance at high temperatures by promoting the in situ formation of a protective alumina (Al2O3) scale while preserving its inherent room‐temperature ductility and high‐temperature yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strengths of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Add approximately 2 atomic percent Al during alloy production to obtain a modified HfNbTaTiZr composition.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at 800 °C for a duration of 5 hours; mechanical loading conditions corresponding to strain rates of 10^(-4)–10^(-2) s^(-1) and room-temperature testing.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent alumina (Al2O3) layer on the surface of the alloy.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum has a high affinity for oxygen and will preferentially oxidize to form Al2O3. This protective scale is known to slow oxygen ingress and reduce further oxidation (pesting) without significantly altering the high-entropy solid-solution microstructure that underpins the alloy’s good mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Al-doped alloy is expected to exhibit significantly improved oxidation resistance (reduced pesting and oxide growth) during 5-hour air exposures at 800 °C while maintaining ductility in the cast condition and high-temperature yield strength comparable to the untreated alloy.
generation.baseline: Untreated, equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr, which in its current state shows inadequate oxygen resistance and undergoes pesting upon exposure to air at elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: This intervention and its beneficial outcomes are anticipated to hold for as-cast samples exposed in air up to 800 °C for durations around 5 hours and under loading conditions similar to those used in prior mechanical tests (strain rates between 10^(-4) and 10^(-2) s^(-1)).
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal amount of Al addition is uncertain, as is the potential for minor detrimental changes in phase stability or microstructural features that might subtly affect ductility or yield strength. Further experimental verification is needed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples – one batch of the standard equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and another with an addition of approximately 2 at.% Al. Expose both batches to ambient air at 800 °C for 5 hours. Subsequently, evaluate the surface oxide characteristics, overall extent of oxidation (e.g., weight gain, oxide thickness), and measure mechanical properties via room-temperature tensile tests and high-temperature yield strength tests.
measurements: Surface oxide layer thickness (using scanning electron microscopy or X-ray diffraction)
Microstructural analysis of the oxide scale (to confirm the formation of Al2O3)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-modified alloy does not show a significant reduction in oxidation (i.e., formation of a protective alumina scale, lower weight gain, thinner or less continuous oxide layer) compared to the untreated alloy, or if the addition of Al leads to unacceptable degradation of ductility or high-temperature yield strength, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractIn as-cast (AC) or heat-treated (HT) metallic ultra-high temperature materials often “conventional” and complex-concentrated (CC) or high-entropy (HE) solid solutions (sss) are observed. Refractory metal containing bcc sss also are contaminated with oxygen. This paper studied the stability of CC/HE Nbss and the contamination with oxygen of Nbss in RM(INb)ICs, RM(Nb)ICs/RCCAs and RM(Nb)ICs/RHEAs. “Conventional” and CC/HE Nbss were compared. “Conventional” Nbss can be Ti-rich only in AC alloys. Ti-rich Nbss is not observed in HT alloys. In B containing alloys the Ti-rich Nbss is usually CC/HE. The CC/HE Nbss is stable in HT alloys with simultaneous addition of Mo, W with Hf, Ge+Sn. The implications for alloy design of correlations between the parameter δ of “conventional” and CC/HE Nbss with the B or the Ge+Sn concentration in the Nbss and of relationships of other solutes with the B or Ge+Sn content are discussed. The CC/HE Nbss has low Δχ, VEC and Ω and high ΔSmix, |ΔHmix| and δ parameters, and is formed in alloys that have high entropy of mixing.
